frameworks.name: Ad Effectiveness Six-Factor Scorecard
frameworks.definition: Alex Hormozi's framework for evaluating ads across six dimensions: (1) did it grab attention, (2) did it make you care, (3) did it sell the dream, (4) did it create urgency, (5) did it show social proof, and (6) did it tell you what to do next.

frameworks.name: Brand Equation Formula
frameworks.definition: A branding structure where the brand is explicitly equated to a value (e.g., Jeep = Freedom), that value is then equated to things the target demo already likes, creating a chain of association that transfers sentiment to the brand.

claims.text: According to Alex Hormozi, effective branding ads work by constructing an explicit equation: Brand = Core Value, then Core Value = things the target demographic already likes, so that the audience's pre-existing positive sentiment transfers to the brand. The Jeep 2026 Super Bowl ad exemplified this by equating Jeep to freedom, then spending the entire runtime equating freedom to specific things their research indicated their conservative, pro-military, outdoors-leaning demographic values.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: branding-objective ads (not direct response)
audience has strong pre-existing values to borrow
claims.mechanism: Pre-existing audience sentiment for the intermediate value (e.g. freedom) transfers to the brand through the associative equation, conditioning purchasing behavior without requiring rational product argument.
bounded_by: Does not apply to direct-response ads where rational product arguments are the mechanism
Fails when the values chosen do not match the actual target demographic's preferences

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that ads which demonstrate product usage throughout the narrative are more effective than ads that build brand sentiment without showing the product in context, because viewers understand what the product does and can connect emotion to the offer. The 2026 Google Gemini ad earned an S-tier rating over the Rocket Mortgage ad (which Hormozi rated A+) primarily because Gemini wove product demonstration throughout its emotional narrative, while Rocket's narrative had no product touchpoints until a one-second end card.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brand-narrative ads with emotional storytelling structure
claims.mechanism: Product demonstration during an emotional arc links the felt emotion to the product in memory; without demonstration, the emotion is experienced but not attributed to the brand.
bounded_by: Urgency creation may not be on-brand for all advertisers even when demonstration is absent

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that crowdsourced advertising — where a brand invites its audience to create ads and selects the winner by engagement data — produces higher-quality, more authentic creatives at lower cost than traditional agency production, because the creators are actual product users who understand the product more deeply than agency employees.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brand with an established, passionate customer base willing to create content
contest format with meaningful prize (e.g., $1M award)
claims.mechanism: Customers who use the product encode authentic product knowledge into the creative; this intimate knowledge produces more believable, resonant advertising than agency work from non-users. Contest upvoting pre-validates creative quality using audience data before broadcast.

numbers.axis: Cost of ad production relative to outcome quality

anchors.value: $1M prize to winner, near-zero production cost, pre-validated by fan upvote

bounded_by: Requires a product with a passionate enough fanbase to generate quality contest submissions
Does not apply to new product categories with no existing user community

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the winning creative from a large-scale audience vote or sharing contest is effectively a pre-tested ad, because the data signal from millions of choices identifies the strongest creative before broadcast, eliminating the guesswork inherent in agency opinion-based selection.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: contest pool large enough to produce statistically meaningful engagement signal
claims.mechanism: Audience voting and sharing behavior is a real-world engagement proxy; the top-voted creative has already demonstrated its ability to capture and hold attention at scale before any media spend is committed.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that ad effectiveness must be judged relative to whether the evaluator is the intended avatar for the ad. If a viewer is not in the target demographic, their negative reaction to an ad is not informative about that ad's effectiveness with its actual target audience.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies when evaluating ads from outside the target demographic
Ramp.com example: only relevant signal from business owners, not general consumers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that branding ads targeting a specific demographic should be built around values and associations drawn from actual customer research on that segment, not from creative team intuition, particularly when media spend is high enough to justify rigorous avatar analysis.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: media spend high enough to justify pre-production customer research (e.g., Super Bowl scale)
claims.mechanism: Customer research reveals which specific values, phrases, and visual scenarios resonate most with the target segment; embedding those validated signals into the creative increases the probability of sentiment transfer to the brand.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that branding ads showing primarily negative imagery (suffering, illness, overweight people) without balancing with aspirational dream-outcome imagery are less effective at changing behavior because the target audience dislikes being reminded of their problem state without seeing a compelling vision of the desired state.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ads targeting audiences with stigmatized or shame-adjacent conditions (e.g., obesity, illness)
claims.mechanism: Audiences with shame-adjacent conditions are motivated by aspiration toward the desired state (dream outcome), not by amplification of the pain state they are already aware of; dwelling on the pain without the dream risks alienating rather than activating.
bounded_by: Fear-based hooks at the opening of an ad are acceptable as attention mechanics before transitioning to dream outcome

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an ad that requires re-watching to understand its message has effectively failed, because most viewers will not re-watch and the moment of potential persuasion is lost. He applied this to the 2026 GoDaddy Super Bowl ad.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: broadcast advertising contexts where re-exposure is not guaranteed
claims.mechanism: Attention in broadcast advertising is non-renewable; a viewer who loses the narrative thread will not rewind a live broadcast, so any confusion mid-ad forfeits all remaining persuasion opportunity.
bounded_by: Digital ads with replay controls may tolerate more complexity

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the most compelling segment of a problem/solution ad is the five to ten seconds immediately before the call-to-action — showing the clearest, most relatable instance of the problem being solved — and that an ad heavy on brand entertainment that ends with a brief, clear solution-CTA pair is structurally superior to one that leads with brand entertainment and buries or omits the problem-solution demonstration.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: direct-response or hybrid brand/direct-response ads
claims.mechanism: The CTA converts viewers who are in active consideration mode; placing the most salient problem-solution demonstration immediately before the CTA captures viewers at peak decision readiness.
bounded_by: Pure brand ads with no CTA intent are exempt from this structure

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that brand-first ads succeed by making the brand synonymous with a value the target audience already holds, rather than by listing product features or price points; the explicit feature/price approach is categorically incompatible with a brand-building objective because it repositions the brand as a commodity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ad campaigns with a brand-building (not direct-response) objective
bounded_by: Direct-response ads appropriately lead with price and features
Hybrid ads can include a feature demonstration while preserving brand sentiment if done carefully (e.g., Google Gemini)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ads targeting an audience should focus on what the audience wants (their dream outcome) rather than on what the advertiser does or offers, because audiences are self-interested and attention follows self-relevance. He identified this as the key failure of the 2026 On (Roger Federer) ad, which focused on the brand name and celebrity rather than on what the audience wants from the product.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any ad targeting an audience that does not already have strong brand familiarity and affinity
claims.mechanism: Audiences process advertising through the filter of self-interest; ads that speak primarily about the brand or product name provide no self-relevant hook and lose attention rapidly.
bounded_by: Established brands with hyper-loyal audiences may sustain attention through brand name alone in limited contexts

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that Nike's brand strength derives from consistently pairing the brand with elite, culturally recognized winners (athletes considered the best in the world or best of all time in their sport), so that purchasing Nike products allows consumers to psychologically approximate their proximity to those winners. This association strategy works because it targets a core human desire to identify with greatness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brand with resources to sign elite athletes
consumer audience that admires competitive achievement
claims.mechanism: Consumers buy branded products to access the emotional identity of the people associated with the brand; proximity-to-greatness desire translates into purchase behavior when the brand is unambiguously paired with recognized winners.
bounded_by: Does not work if the brand simultaneously claims all consumers are winners, because that dilutes the exclusive-excellence association (Hormozi cites The Incredibles: if everyone is a winner, no one is)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a brand built on winning as its core identity cannot simultaneously claim that everyone is a winner, because that claim destroys the brand's core value proposition: if winning is universal, the brand conveys no aspirational distinctiveness.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: brands whose core identity is built on competitive achievement or exclusivity
claims.mechanism: The value of a winning-identity brand is aspirational scarcity; universalizing the winning claim collapses that scarcity and removes the reason consumers pay a premium to be associated with the brand.
bounded_by: Brands built on inclusivity or participation (not elite performance) are not subject to this constraint

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that ad creative for a service or tool targeting small business owners should feature actual small business owners in relatable business situations, not actors or celebrities in analogous roles, because small business owners do not identify with actors and the actor framing creates irrelevance for the intended audience. He applied this to the 2026 GoDaddy ad.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ads targeting small business owners or other practitioner segments
product is a practical tool, not an aspirational lifestyle product
bounded_by: Aspirational lifestyle products (athletic gear, luxury goods) can use celebrity association effectively

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a high-text, subtitle-heavy visual presentation is superior to audio-only calls to action for television ads, because many viewers watch from a distance and cannot reliably hear or parse audio-only text, particularly for brand or product names they are unfamiliar with.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: television broadcast ads
product or brand name that is not yet well-known to the mass audience
bounded_by: Radio and podcast formats where visual text is unavailable

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an ad structure modeled as: high-volume attention-grabbing content → fact that creates discomfort → testimonial of someone who avoided the negative outcome using the product → clear CTA is a replicable, high-effectiveness template applicable across many business categories, not just healthcare. He identified the 2026 Novartis breast cancer screening ad as exemplifying this structure.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ads for products that solve a problem with high negative consequence if ignored
audience is likely unaware of their personal risk
bounded_by: Ad must still drive behavior change, not just positive sentiment; if the tone is too entertaining, viewers may leave feeling good without taking action

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an Americana-themed branding ad (featuring military, American dream, home ownership, and regional American imagery) is most effective when run during the Super Bowl because the Super Bowl audience is itself an Americana cultural event, making the emotional context of the broadcast congruent with the ad's associative content. He applied this to the 2026 Rocket Mortgage ad.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Americana or patriotism-themed brand narrative
broadcast context: Super Bowl or equivalent culturally American event
claims.mechanism: Contextual congruence between the broadcast environment and the ad's associative content amplifies sentiment transfer; the audience is already in an emotionally activated, Americana-receptive state during the Super Bowl.
bounded_by: Americana messaging will only resonate with audiences who identify with the American dream narrative; international or urban-cosmopolitan audiences may not be activated

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a branding ad that ends with a CTA so brief or visually understated that viewers cannot identify the brand or product category has failed at its primary business objective even if the narrative content is emotionally compelling, because unattributed positive sentiment does not convert to sales or brand recall. He rated the 2026 Rocket Mortgage ad A+ (not S tier) for exactly this reason.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Positive sentiment toward an ad creates purchase intent only if the viewer can attribute that sentiment to a specific brand or product; an unrecognized CTA breaks the attribution chain and the emotional work of the ad is wasted.

examples.text: The 2026 Google Gemini Super Bowl ad built a brief but complete emotional story arc — akin to the opening sequence of the film Up — weaving product demonstration (a job candidate using Gemini to practice interview answers) throughout a sentimental human narrative about career growth and belonging. The product was visible and in use at every emotional beat, so viewers understood both what the product does and felt positive emotion while watching it do it. Alex Hormozi rated this S tier and used it as the benchmark against which all other ads were measured.

Doritos' 2026 Super Bowl ad was created by a fan through a public contest. Doritos offered a $1 million prize for the winning fan-submitted ad. The winning ad contained almost no words and relied entirely on visual storytelling — showing someone risking danger to protect a bag of Doritos, then resolving to a moment of sharing. Hormozi estimated that traditional ad agency production for an equivalent ad would cost more than $1 million without the pre-validation of audience selection. Because fans voted and shared the ad to determine the winner, the eventual broadcast ad was already proven to capture attention at scale before a dollar of media was spent. Hormozi rated it an A.

The 2026 Ramp.com Super Bowl ad (approximately 15 seconds) opened with a pain-based question relevant to the football audience — whether to pull a star player off the field to submit his expenses — and immediately resolved the pain by showing the product's solution. Hormozi noted the hook was contextually relevant to the Super Bowl audience, that the problem-to-solution demonstration was completed within the allotted time, and rated it an A. His only critique was that the CTA appeared only in audio rather than on-screen text, which he considered a missed opportunity given TV viewing distances.

The 2026 Jeep Super Bowl ad ran approximately two minutes, spending the full runtime naming things their research-informed avatar (conservative, pro-military, outdoors-oriented) values under the umbrella of freedom: veterans, family, independence, rural America, and the right to choose. No pricing, no financing terms, and no product features were mentioned. Harrison Ford appeared at the end in a brief, lighthearted moment referencing his last name. Hormozi rated the ad an A, citing the clarity of the brand equation (Jeep = Freedom = things you already love) and the specificity of the value choices as evidence of rigorous customer research.

The 2026 Hims & Hers Super Bowl ad opened with jarring footage of overweight people and mortality statistics, then pivoted to criticizing the healthcare system for prioritizing profit over patients, then ended with a pitch for Hims & Hers weight loss medications as the solution. Hormozi rated it D, identifying three specific failures: (1) the ad showed the problem state (overweight people) extensively but showed almost no dream-outcome imagery of people who had successfully lost weight; (2) the attack on pharmaceutical industry profit followed immediately by a pitch for their own medications felt self-contradictory and reduced credibility; (3) the brand attempted to reposition itself as a healthcare company in the same ad, creating identity confusion rather than a clear association.

The 2026 GoDaddy Super Bowl ad spent approximately two-thirds of its runtime showing actor Walton Goggins in various roles (detective, astronaut) pretending to know what he was doing, as an analogy to small business owners who also pretend. Only in the final third was GoDaddy's AI-powered website-building product introduced. Hormozi rated it C, citing two failures: (1) the actor framing prompted him to think the ad did not apply to him, disengaging him early; (2) the structure required re-watching to understand the message. He proposed an alternative structure: show a small business owner failing at 4-5 relatable business tasks, then show GoDaddy solving the one task it actually solves, then revisit the other tasks now resolved, closing with a CTA.

The 2026 Rocket Mortgage Super Bowl ad built an extended Americana narrative — military homecomings, first-time homeowners, different regions of the United States, the American dream — without showing or mentioning mortgages or Rocket until a one-second end card displaying rocket.com. Hormozi rated it A+ but not S tier, explaining that a viewer who was not paying close attention at the final second would not know which company made the ad or what it offered. He contrasted this directly with the Google Gemini ad, where the product was demonstrated throughout the emotional arc, making attribution unambiguous.

The 2026 Nike Super Bowl ad featured exclusively female athletes — widely considered the best in their respective sports — performing and winning while a voiceover listed things women are told they cannot do, then instructed them to do each thing anyway. Hormozi rated it an A, noting that Nike signed athletes widely considered the greatest of all time and that the purchase mechanism is proximity-to-greatness desire: buyers wear Nike to feel they are approximating the champions they admire. He added that Nike's previous drift toward messaging where everyone is a winner had diluted this mechanism, and that this ad's return to competitive excellence restored the brand's core associative power.

The 2026 Novartis breast cancer screening Super Bowl ad used attention-grabbing footage referencing breasts in popular culture (sports, entertainment) before pivoting to the serious message that breasts deserve attention for health screening. It included a testimonial from someone who had undergone early detection and ended with a clear CTA. Hormozi rated it B+, praising the attention mechanic and the testimonial structure, but questioning whether the entertaining tone would drive actual screening appointments. He proposed two alternative versions — a Google Gemini-style narrative about moments you would miss from late detection, or a Jeep-style freedom narrative that ends with a sobering consequence — as potentially more behavior-changing.

practices.text: When evaluating whether an ad worked, ask whether you are actually the target avatar for that ad before rendering a judgment; if you are not the intended demographic, your reaction is not informative.

For television broadcast ads, over-index on on-screen text for product names, CTAs, and key claims rather than relying on audio alone, because many viewers are at a distance and will miss audio-only information.

In a problem-solution ad, structure the final 5-10 seconds as the clearest, most relatable instantiation of the problem being solved, immediately followed by the product name or CTA, so that the peak decision-readiness moment aligns with the ask.

When writing branding ad copy, choose every value, word, and visual from verified customer research data on what the target demographic actually likes rather than from creative team intuition — particularly when media spend justifies the research cost.

For brands with engaged customer communities, consider running a crowdsourced ad contest rather than commissioning agency production; use public upvotes or shares to select the winner so audience data pre-validates the creative before broadcast.
